lesson_title: Two People Counting the Same Money: Bank Reconciliation
hook_text: Your book says R60 800. The bank says R55 650. Nobody is lying.
clip_script: Picture a stokvel. You keep the book at home; the treasurer keeps a book at the bank. Month end, the numbers differ. Nobody stole anything. Nobody is lying. The books differ because two people wrote at two different moments. Same money, two clocks. That is a hardware shop and its bank exactly. But there is a second reason, and this one is not about time: the bank does things to your money without phoning you. It takes its fees. It pays you a little interest. It carries out the standing orders you signed months ago. And if a customer's transfer bounces because their account was empty, the bank quietly takes that money back out. So sort every line on that statement into three piles. News the bank did that you never wrote down — write it into your journals. Your own slips, like a payment of R4 380 written as R3 480 — fix your book. And things you leave completely alone: the deposit that has not cleared, the transfers that have not gone out. Then ask one question for the bridge: what is the bank still going to do to this? Add what it will add, subtract what it will subtract. Both books land on R60 800.
visual_style: A split screen: a home ledger and a bank statement, items flying into three labelled piles, then a bridge drawing itself between two numbers until both read R60 800; warm Limpopo hardware-yard palette with hand-written ledger textures.
pacing: Fast three-pile sort, then a slow bridge build to the matching totals.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and sort every statement line yourself — three piles, one bridge.
